title: Al-Muqit, the Nourisher
hookLine: the Nourisher, who sustains every creature
tomorrow: why does a verse about saying hello end with God counting?

cards: A granola bar eaten one-handed over a keyboard. Lunch as a pit stop. The Qur'an has a scene about food nobody planned.
In Surah Al Imran, a young woman, Maryam, lives in the sanctuary, promised to God's service by her mother before she was born. Her guardian is the old prophet Zakariyya, the one responsible for her.
Every time he walks in to check on her, there's food beside her. He didn't bring it. Nobody he knows brought it.
One day he finally asks: O Maryam, where did this come from?

teach.b: Her answer is short. In Pickthall's translation: "It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will." No menu, no explanation.

Just where it came from: not from Zakariyya, not from luck, not from her own planning. That answer opens today's Name: Al-Muqit, the Nourisher. You meet it in Surah An-Nisa, and in the list of Names in Jami' at-Tirmidhi.
Scholars have heard it two ways.
Some say al-Muqit sends each creature the food that keeps it going. Others say it's the one who watches over all things and holds them up.

teach.h: BODIES WITH FOOD, HEARTS WITH KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: Al-Ghazali, writing on the Names, held both together, and added the detail worth telling a friend tonight: the Nourisher feeds bodies with food, and hearts with knowledge. So the scene in the sanctuary feeds both.

Maryam has a plate, and she knows where it's from. And Zakariyya, standing there, gets hungry for something else: in the very next verse, he prays for a child of his own. Muslims carry this into an ordinary lunch.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once told a boy eating at his table: say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you.
Three small things that turn a pit stop into a meal you notice. Bismillah first. Then taste.

how: Muslims learn to say bismillah before eating, to eat with the right hand and from what is near, following a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari; Al-Muqit is called on in du'a among the Names in Jami' at-Tirmidhi's list.

o: the one who sets the times of daily prayer
the Nourisher, who sends what keeps you going
the one who cooks for the poor at feasts

games.q: who's who in the sanctuary — tap the pairs.
p: her guardian, who asked where it came from
bodies with food, hearts with knowledge

s: scholars agree Al-Muqit has only one meaning
some hear the Nourisher, others the one who watches over all things; al-Ghazali held both.
Zakariyya was the one bringing Maryam her food
he found it there, and asked her where it came from (3:37).
the Prophet ﷺ taught a boy to say Allah's name before eating
say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, eat from what's near you (Sahih al-Bukhari).

games.q: your cousin eats dinner standing at the fridge, phone in hand, every night. your aunt asks you to help. which ask fits today's lesson?
o: 'sit with us for the first few bites. bismillah, then taste it.'
'eat however you want. God feeds you either way.'
'skip dinner till homework's done. hunger keeps you sharp.'
games.why: the Prophet's ﷺ three small manners, Allah's name, the right hand, what's near, turn eating into noticing where the food came from. that's al-Muqit at the table.

practice: If there's something to eat or drink near you, a piece of fruit, a cup of tea, even a glass of water, hold it first. Notice its smell and its weight, and the hands that grew it or carried it here.
Say bismillah, then take one slow bite or sip, and let it stay a moment before you swallow. Then rest your hands for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Muqit. The Nourisher, who sends each creature what keeps it going, and feeds bodies with food and hearts with knowledge. Name thirty-nine.

orig.note: Arabic: the Nourisher; also read as the one who watches over all things. it appears in Surah An-Nisa (4:85).

carryVoice: Keep this: nourished, because Maryam's plate came from somewhere, and so does yours. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:35–38 (Maryam's mother's vow, Zakariyya as guardian, the food in the sanctuary, Zakariyya's prayer for a child)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5376 (say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, eat from what is near you)
al-Ghazali, al-Maqsad al-Asna, on al-Muqit (nourishment for bodies as food, for hearts as knowledge)
sources.work: al-Maqsad al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna
